explanations.explanation: A warning it is, friend. God tells Ezekiel, "Whenever you hear a word from My mouth, give them a warning from Me." (Ezekiel 3:17) Think of a smoke alarm. Nobody calls it rude for beeping, because beeping is the whole job. Ezekiel's job is to pass along what he hears from God.

I'd sign up for the blessing job in a heartbeat, but that's not what God hands Ezekiel. He says, "Whenever you hear a word from My mouth, give them a warning from Me." (Ezekiel 3:17) The word that comes to Ezekiel is a warning. Nice guess, though, baker. Your heart is in the right kitchen.

A song! I can picture the choir robes already. But the text says no encore here. God says, "Whenever you hear a word from My mouth, give them a warning from Me." (Ezekiel 3:17) The watchman's job is a warning, not a hit single.

This is a heavy part of the passage, so let's go slowly. The text says the opposite. If Ezekiel doesn't warn him, "that wicked man will die in his iniquity, and I will hold you responsible for his blood." (Ezekiel 3:18) The man is not let off, and Ezekiel is the one God says He will hold responsible.

Right, and this is a heavy part of the passage. God says that if Ezekiel doesn't warn him, "that wicked man will die in his iniquity, and I will hold you responsible for his blood." (Ezekiel 3:18) The man still dies in his iniquity. Ezekiel's silence doesn't change that, and God says Ezekiel is the one He will hold responsible.

Ezekiel is the answer. God says it straight to him: "I will hold you responsible for his blood." (Ezekiel 3:18) The "you" there is Ezekiel, the watchman. I think that's a lot to hear, and God said it plainly.

The elders don't show up anywhere in these verses. God is speaking right to Ezekiel when He says, "I will hold you responsible for his blood." (Ezekiel 3:18) That "you" is the watchman himself. I think that's a weighty thing to hear, and God says it plainly.

His family isn't mentioned in this verse at all. God speaks straight to Ezekiel: "I will hold you responsible for his blood." (Ezekiel 3:18) The "you" is the watchman, not the man's relatives. I think that's a serious thing to hear, and God says it plainly.

That's what God says: "you will have saved yourself." (Ezekiel 3:19) Ezekiel warned the man, and the man did not turn from his wickedness. He will die in his iniquity, yet Ezekiel has done what God asked. It's a sober verse, and I think the way God lays out each case is very clear.

The text says the opposite for Ezekiel. When he warns the wicked man and the man doesn't turn, God says, "you will have saved yourself." (Ezekiel 3:19) The man dies in his iniquity, but Ezekiel isn't pulled in with him. Ezekiel did his part by warning.

The verse doesn't say that. It says, "he will die in his iniquity, but you will have saved yourself." (Ezekiel 3:19) That is where the warning leaves Ezekiel, and it is the end of the line for this case. I'm only telling you what the text states, baker, and it states that he has saved himself.

The text says otherwise, and it's a sobering line. When a righteous man turns to iniquity and nobody warned him, "the righteous acts he did will not be remembered." (Ezekiel 3:20) God also says again, "I will hold you responsible for his blood." So the warning matters a great deal in this case.

That's right, and it's a sobering line. God says the righteous man "will die in his sin, and the righteous acts he did will not be remembered." (Ezekiel 3:20) That's about the man who was not warned. God also says again, "I will hold you responsible for his blood."

He lives, friend. God says, "he will indeed live because he heeded your warning, and you will have saved yourself." (Ezekiel 3:21) A warning is given, a warning is heard, and a life goes on. That's the best batch of the four cases.

explanations.answer: He will die in his sin
explanations.explanation: That's the case before this one. In the third case, nobody warned the righteous man, and God says "he will die in his sin." (Ezekiel 3:20) This time Ezekiel warns him, and the man does not sin. God says, "he will indeed live because he heeded your warning." (Ezekiel 3:21)

explanations.answer: He is cut off from Israel
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions anyone being cut off. It says this man "will indeed live because he heeded your warning, and you will have saved yourself." (Ezekiel 3:21) He was warned not to sin, and he doesn't sin. So his outcome is life.

True. Ezekiel goes out to the plain and says, "the glory of the LORD was present there, like the glory I had seen by the River Kebar, and I fell facedown." (Ezekiel 3:23) Nobody had to push him. Some things are bigger than a person standing up.

The plain doesn't stay quiet for him. Ezekiel says, "the glory of the LORD was present there, like the glory I had seen by the River Kebar, and I fell facedown." (Ezekiel 3:23) So he does go down on his face. The text says it just that plainly.

explanations.answer: Into his house to shut himself in
explanations.explanation: Home it is. After the Spirit sets him on his feet, He says, "Go, shut yourself inside your house." (Ezekiel 3:24) A watchman sent indoors, and I'd have bet on a wall too, friend. Good thing the text keeps us honest.

explanations.answer: Up onto the city wall to watch
explanations.explanation: Watchman, wall, it sounds just right, and I'd have bet on it too. But the Spirit says, "Go, shut yourself inside your house." (Ezekiel 3:24) The order points indoors, not up a wall. The text surprises us on this one, baker.

The temple isn't in this passage. After the Spirit sets Ezekiel on his feet, He says, "Go, shut yourself inside your house." (Ezekiel 3:24) That's the next order, and it sends him home. Nice try, friend.

That's it. God says, "you will be silent and unable to rebuke them, though they are a rebellious house." (Ezekiel 3:26) Ever had cookie dough stuck to the roof of your mouth? Hard to say much of anything. Ezekiel's tongue is stuck, so he can't rebuke them.

The tongue is about speaking, not hearing. God says, "you will be silent and unable to rebuke them." (Ezekiel 3:26) God also says, "when I speak with you, I will open your mouth." (Ezekiel 3:27) So the LORD still speaks with him. It's the rebuking that his stuck tongue stops.

Eyes are fine, baker. The stuck tongue is about his words. God says, "you will be silent and unable to rebuke them, though they are a rebellious house." (Ezekiel 3:26) The verse says nothing about him seeing the glory again, so I won't add it.

True. God finishes with, "Whoever listens, let him listen; and whoever refuses, let him refuse, for they are a rebellious house." (Ezekiel 3:27) Ezekiel gets to say "This is what the Lord GOD says," and that's his job. Some will hear it and some won't.

It's right there in the verse, friend. God says, "Whoever listens, let him listen; and whoever refuses, let him refuse, for they are a rebellious house." (Ezekiel 3:27) So the statement is true. Ezekiel is told to say, "This is what the Lord GOD says," and the people's response is theirs.
